beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe by looking at its output.
beats.got: Looking at output isn't enough to know an agent is safe. That's a fair point, but I'd rather not hear it as a slogan.

beats.trigger: Read [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain)
beats.got: The patterns I get to look at are indirect injection and skill supply chain. Those are new to me.

beats.trigger: You've had three agents search your company and three more decide.
beats.got: A bunch of agents deciding with nobody checking is exactly the thing I'd worry about with sales or HR near it.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent which tools it can use right now.
beats.got: nothing new. I know how tool calls work and I'd skip it.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years
beats.got: nothing new. This paragraph is brochure filler.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is plain English in a document the agent reads, and it uses access the agent already has. My perimeter thinking doesn't cover that.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels).
beats.got: Scope, split, filter, gate and review are a tidy set of mitigations I can name for agents.

beats.trigger: "Hope it doesn't happen" is not one.
beats.got: Residual risk gets written down and either accepted or closed. That's sensible, a bit ceremonial.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a pep talk.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable check the agent loads. I already half knew that, but it's a useful frame for the security check.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked from files and some need a human or evidence. I didn't have that split before.

beats.trigger: Tell the agent what matters about your company's policies and the agent system you built in modules 2-3.
beats.got: I tell the agent which data would hurt us if it leaked, before it reads the files. Fine, but it's a chore.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose
beats.got: The agent interviews me and writes a two-lens skill. I like that I can hand the rest back.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: When I have no view I can delegate with 'optimise for what I can't steer'. I'll reuse that line.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/security-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: nothing new. It's install steps.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: The skill is the thing to keep, not the policy files. Fair.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The audit isn't meant to pass. It's meant to run the loop once on my own system.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: My own check will flag things I assumed were fine and mark some as 'can't tell'. I'd have signed those off by eye.

beats.trigger: Two different lenses; some risks will overlap, some will not.
beats.got: Two lenses give two different risk lists. I can talk through each risk with the agent and look at what a failure would actually look like.

beats.trigger: A mitigation reduces, it does not eliminate.
beats.got: One mitigation, then a written residual I accept on record. I'd have called one fix good enough and moved on.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent.
beats.got: Risk control is part of what makes something production. I agree, but it's two lines and thin.

beats.trigger: the root instructions file now tells future sessions how to behave around the risk you found.
beats.got: The finding goes back into the instructions file, so the next session starts stricter. That's the part I could use across a whole org.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is the easiest way to hand a method to a teammate. It doesn't solve who owns it, though.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: nothing new beyond the recap.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework: one sentence per case on the missing check. I'd probably wing it.

beats.trigger: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases of an agent's output going out with no check around it. I'll read them if I get time.

take_homes: Prompt injection through documents the agent reads is the real attack surface. My firewall thinking doesn't cover it.
Agent-specific mitigations are scope, split, filter, gate and review. Every one still leaves a written residual risk.
A skill that runs the check, plus the debrief writing rules back into the instructions file, is the reusable part.

monday.move: Run the security-audit skill on the weekend sales-team agent setup, and check who maintains it before building more.
monday.who: me, then the one person who would own it
monday.when: Monday evening, probably after the kids are in bed
monday.stop_condition: I have one named residual risk and a named owner, or I drop the sales setup
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering asked for it, and I'd want to skip straight to building the next thing.

misconception.why: I assumed some things were settled and the check left them as 'I can't tell'. I still think review steps are slow for strong output, but I can't say my own eyeballing was enough.

one_line: The middle bit on injection and the 'I can't tell' rows was worth it. The first half is slow if you already run agents, and I'd skip the tool-loop demo.
